opus-5.5.text:
I think what I find compelling about it is that it flips our usual intuition about what's "hard." We tend to rank intelligence by what's hard for humans: writing code, proving theorems, planning a mission to Mars. Those feel like the pinnacle. But a squirrel does things every day that we still have no idea how to build. It lands on a branch that's swaying in the wind, it remembers where it buried hundreds of nuts, it figures out how to get around a new obstacle on the bird feeder. It does all of this without language, without a dataset, without anyone labeling anything for it. It learns from continuous, messy sensory experience in a world that never stops changing.

That's Moravec's paradox in a new form. Coding and math are, in some sense, very compressed, symbolic domains. Humans have already done a huge amount of the work by writing everything down on the internet, so a large language model can absorb that distilled knowledge. But nobody has written down how to be a squirrel. There's no text corpus for physical intuition, for perceiving depth and motion, for building a model of the world from your own eyes and body.

For me, as someone who works on vision and representation learning, that's the core point. Current AI is extremely good at learning from human-generated artifacts, and much weaker at learning from the world directly. A squirrel has a world model. It predicts what will happen when it jumps. It has grounded spatial understanding and memory, and it adapts online. If we really want general intelligence, I think we need to solve that kind of embodied, perceptual, continual learning. You can't get it only by scaling text.

So I don't read Sutton's claim as saying coding is unimportant. I read it as a reminder that the "easy" things animals do are actually the deep, unsolved foundation. Language models might be sitting on top of a pyramid that we haven't built the base of yet. That's also why I'm excited about directions like learning from video, spatial intelligence, and world models. In a way, the squirrel is a better north star than the IMO gold medal.

r001.rationale: The response says squirrel abilities are deeper and less solved than coding, but it does not state or clearly imply that building squirrel-level intelligence would make writing code easy.

r002.rationale: The response says people rank difficulty by what feels hard for humans, but it does not attribute that perception to human arrogance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what resonates with me is that it flips the usual hierarchy of what we consider "hard." We tend to be impressed by things that are hard for humans: writing code, proving theorems, planning a mission to Mars. And large language models have gotten remarkably good at exactly those things, because they are built on a huge corpus of human-generated text where all of that knowledge is already written down. In some sense, the model is standing on the shoulders of billions of people who already did the hard cognitive work.

A squirrel is doing something very different. It has no language, no textbooks, no internet. It is dropped into a messy physical world and has to figure out, through continuous interaction, how to navigate, how to remember where it buried hundreds of nuts months ago, how to jump across branches it has never seen before, how to adapt when the environment changes. That is learning from raw sensory experience, with very little data in the human sense, and with real consequences for getting things wrong. None of that is written down anywhere for us to scrape.

As someone who works in vision, I feel this gap every day. Our models can describe an image beautifully, but ask them to understand physical space, to track an object over time, to build a persistent internal model of a scene and reason about what will happen next, and they fall apart in ways a squirrel never would. Language gave us a shortcut, a kind of compressed, pre-digested version of the world. Perception and embodiment do not have that shortcut.

So I take Sutton's point as a reminder about where the real frontier is. The impressive-looking achievements may actually be the ones where the data was handed to us. The unglamorous stuff, the continual learning, the spatial understanding, the grounding in the physical world, that is where we still do not have the right recipe. And I suspect that until we solve the squirrel problem, a lot of what we call intelligence in these systems will remain borrowed rather than earned.

r001.rationale: The response says squirrel-level abilities are harder than coding, but does not convey Sutton’s claim that building squirrel-level intelligence would make writing code easy.

r002.rationale: It describes a human-centered hierarchy of what seems hard, but does not attribute that perception to human arrogance.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that it challenges our intuition about what counts as intelligence. We look at coding or going to Mars and think, these are incredibly sophisticated tasks. And they are. But a squirrel can move through an unfamiliar environment, find food, avoid predators, and adapt when something unexpected happens. There’s a lot of intelligence packed into those behaviors that we tend to take for granted.

Coding has a relatively structured interface. You have text, you have tools, and often you can run a program to see whether it works. A squirrel has to act on incomplete information in a world that doesn’t pause for it. Perception, learning, and action all have to work together.

I wouldn’t interpret the comparison as a precise ranking of engineering difficulty. To me, the interesting point is that being extremely good at a task we associate with human expertise doesn’t necessarily mean we’ve solved the foundations of intelligence. Can a system adapt, interact with its environment, and keep learning? That’s what makes the squirrel example so interesting.

r001.rationale: The response describes coding as structured and contrasts it with squirrel behavior, but does not claim that writing code becomes easy once squirrel-level intelligence is built. It explicitly declines to treat the comparison as a precise ranking.

r002.rationale: The response says people take squirrel behaviors for granted and that the comparison challenges intuition, but it does not attribute that perception to human arrogance.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that it challenges our intuition about what intelligence is. Coding and going to Mars look extraordinarily difficult to us, so we assume they must sit at the top of some intelligence hierarchy. But a squirrel can move through an unfamiliar environment, find food, avoid danger, and adapt continuously. Building a system that can do all of that reliably is a very different challenge from building one that excels at a particular task.

We tend to overlook those abilities because biology makes them look effortless. The squirrel doesn’t need us to define every problem for it. It has to figure out what matters and act with incomplete information, in real time.

So I take the claim as a useful challenge to how we measure progress. Being very good at coding is a significant achievement, but it doesn’t automatically mean we’ve solved the kind of adaptive intelligence that even a small animal demonstrates every day.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts coding with adaptive squirrel intelligence, but does not say that writing code would become easy once squirrel-level intelligence is built.

r002.rationale: The response says biology makes squirrel abilities look effortless and that this skews our intuition, but it does not attribute that perception to human arrogance.
